content_html:
Comparing a monthly rent check with a mortgage payment does not tell you whether buying is the better deal. Owning brings extra costs such as property tax, insurance, maintenance and the expense of selling, but it also builds equity and may gain value. Renting is often cheaper month to month and leaves your down payment free to invest. This calculator puts both paths side by side and shows which leaves you with more wealth after the number of years you choose.

How to use this calculator

  1. Buying: enter the home price, down payment, mortgage rate and term, closing costs, property tax rate, insurance, maintenance and any HOA fee.
  2. Renting: enter the monthly rent and renter's insurance for a comparable home.
  3. Assumptions: choose how many years you expect to stay, what your savings could earn if invested, and how fast home prices and rents may rise.
  4. More options: adjust selling costs, the inflation rate for insurance and HOA fees, and the mortgage insurance (PMI) rate for down payments under 20%.

How the comparison works

The calculator runs month by month. The buyer pays the down payment and closing costs up front, then the mortgage payment, property tax, maintenance, insurance, HOA and any PMI. The renter pays rent and renter's insurance and invests the cash the buyer spent up front. Each month, whichever household has the lower housing cost invests the difference at your chosen return. That way both households spend the same amount, and the comparison is fair.

At the end of each year, the buyer's net worth is the home's value minus selling costs, minus the remaining mortgage, plus any investments. The renter's net worth is the investment account. The year in which the buyer first comes out ahead is the break-even point.

Worked example

Take a $400,000 home with 20% down, a 6.5% 30-year mortgage, 3% closing costs, 1.1% property tax, $1,800 a year of insurance and 1% maintenance, compared with renting for $2,200 a month plus $20 of renter's insurance. Buying needs $92,000 in cash, and the mortgage payment is $2,022.62, so owning costs about $2,872.62 a month in the first year versus $2,220 for renting.

With 3% yearly growth in home prices and rent, a 5% investment return and 6% selling costs, the renter is ahead by about $33,753 after one year because of the up-front costs. Buying catches up in year 9, and after 10 years the buyer's net worth is about $234,029 against $222,503 for the renter, a gap of roughly $11,526.

What moves the result most

  • How long you stay: buying and selling costs are large, so short stays usually favor renting.
  • Price growth versus investment return: the gap between these two rates compounds every year.
  • The rent-to-price ratio: when yearly rent is a small share of the home price, renting tends to win.
  • Mortgage rate: a higher rate means more of each payment is interest rather than equity.

Limits of this comparison

  • It ignores income tax effects, including the mortgage interest deduction (which helps only if you itemize) and tax on investment gains.
  • Returns and price growth are steady averages. Real markets move unevenly, so try cautious and optimistic scenarios.
  • It assumes the renter actually invests the savings. If that money would be spent instead, buying looks better than shown.

faq.question: How long do I need to stay in a home for buying to pay off?
faq.answer: It depends on prices, rents and rates where you live, but buying often takes several years to break even because of closing costs on the way in and selling costs on the way out. The break-even year in the results shows the answer for your own numbers.

faq.question: Why does the calculator assume the renter invests money?
faq.answer: A buyer ties up the down payment and closing costs in the home. A fair comparison assumes the renter keeps that cash working, along with any monthly savings from lower housing costs. Without it, renting would look worse than it really is.

faq.question: What investment return should I use?
faq.answer: Use the rate you realistically expect on the money you would otherwise put into a home. A cautious savings account, a balanced portfolio and a stock-heavy portfolio give very different results, so try a few rates.

faq.question: Does the calculator include the mortgage interest tax deduction?
faq.answer: No. Since the standard deduction roughly doubled in 2018, most homeowners no longer itemize, so the deduction often provides little or no benefit. If you do itemize, buying will look somewhat better than shown.

faq.question: Is home equity the same as profit?
faq.answer: No. Equity is the home's value minus what you owe. To turn it into cash you have to sell, which typically costs 5% to 10% of the price in commissions and closing costs. The net worth figures here subtract those selling costs.
